title: Opening Drive
teaches: The opening drive as we trade it: the day-1 entry for a leader above its 200-day, read on 5-minute bars. The first 5-minute bar closes green, the day's low is the open or inside that bar, and price never trades back to the open; the buy is a market order the moment price trades through the first bar's high, never more than 4% past it; the stop sits a few cents under the day's low; the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest on the trail; a stop-out is the plan working, and the second entry is the first light-volume pullback that holds VWAP.

facts.quote: A stock gaps up or down on earnings and drives strongly in one direction during the first few minutes of the Open.
facts.claim: SMB: after a gap on news, the stock drives strongly in one direction in the first few minutes.

facts.quote: Let’s define what we mean by an Opening Drive Play. This is a momentum trade right on the open, right after 9:30AM.
facts.claim: SMB: the Opening Drive Play is a momentum trade right on the open, right after 9:30.

facts.quote: Generally when there is going to be a good opening drive it happens right away.

facts.quote: It is unusual for there to be a delay of 5-6 minutes.

facts.quote: You are either in a Scalp Opening Drive Play with all its specific exits or a Trade2Hold Opening Drive Play.
facts.claim: SMB: you are in a scalp or a hold plan, chosen before the entry.

facts.quote: you almost never want to start a Trade2Hold on the open because stocks do not trend on the open

facts.quote: You should see a price surge and elevated volume right after the opening bell rings.
facts.claim: SMB: a drive shows a price surge and elevated volume right after the bell.

facts.quote: After a strong Opening Drive, we want to see a pull in on light volume, and a hold above VWAP.
facts.claim: SMB: after a strong drive, the pullback is on light volume and holds above VWAP.

questions.q: Where's your buy on this one?
questions.why: The first 5-minute bar's high. That's the trigger on a drive. I mark that high the second the bar closes. The buy is a market order the moment price trades through it. The full 9:30 to 10:00 range is the ORB, the opening range breakout. That's the slow version of the same morning, for days that don't drive. Yesterday's high is a Kicker's line. The open is just one print, not a level anyone's defending. Here the bar closed green with the low of the day inside it, so the 5-minute high is your line.
questions.lesson_line: Mark the first 5-minute high. The trade through it is your buy.

wrong.The first 30-minute bar's high: That's the ORB's level, the slow version of the morning. A drive doesn't wait for it.
wrong.Yesterday's high: That's a Kicker's line, over a red day's high. A drive reads today's first bar.
wrong.The opening print: The open is one price, not a level. You need a bar's high to trade through.

questions.simple: The first 5-minute bar's high. You buy the moment price trades through it.

reasons: the 5-minute trigger bar rests on a proposed card line tied to held decision D-031

questions.story: A leader above its 200-day gaps up at the open. The first 5-minute bar closes green, and the low of the day sits inside it.

questions.q: A stock gaps up, runs for a bit, then makes its low of the day at 11:15. That still counts as an opening drive.
questions.why: False. On a real drive the low of the day, LOD for short, is set in the first few minutes. It's the open, or it sits inside the first 5-minute bar. That's the whole idea. Buyers show up at the bell and never let it trade back down. A low at 11:15 means sellers had the stock for well over an hour. That's not a drive. And if you'd bought early, a new low under your fill is just your stop getting hit, the plan doing its job.
questions.lesson_line: A drive makes its low at the bell. A late low means it wasn't one.
questions.simple: False. A real drive sets its low at the open or in the first 5-minute bar, not late in the morning.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)

questions.q: Where's your stop?
choices: A few cents under the low of the day
Right on the first bar's low
questions.answer: A few cents under the low of the day
questions.why: A few cents under the low of the day. On a drive that low is the open or the bottom of the first 5-minute bar, so it's close and it's tight. That's the spot that proves you wrong. If price takes out the low the buyers set at the bell, there's no drive anymore. I put it a few cents under, not right on it. That way a quick tag of the exact low doesn't shake me out. The 50-day and yesterday's close have nothing to do with this morning.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the low of the day. Not on it, under it.

wrong.Just under yesterday's close: Yesterday's close isn't the line. Today's low is where the drive is wrong.
wrong.Under the rising 50-day moving average: Way too far, and it has nothing to do with this morning. The drive's stop is today's low.
wrong.Right on the first bar's low: Close, but not on it. A few cents under, so a tag of the exact low doesn't take you out.

questions.simple: A few cents under the low of the day. That's where the drive is proven wrong.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F62)

questions.story: You just got filled on a drive at 9:35. It was a market order as price traded through the first 5-minute high.

questions.q: The drive already ran before you could act. How far past the trigger is too far to still buy it?
questions.sentence: Once price is more than ___% past the first 5-minute bar's high, I let it go.
questions.why: 4%. Past that, the buy point's gone. Here's why it matters. Your stop doesn't move up with price. It stays a few cents under the low of the day. So every cent you chase stretches the distance to the stop. To keep the same dollar risk, your size has to shrink. Chasing costs you size. Measure it from the first bar's high, not from the open. Past 4%, I wait for the second entry, the first light pullback that holds VWAP.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the trigger, you missed it. Wait for the second entry.
questions.simple: 4. Past that you're chasing, the stop is too far away, and you wait for the second entry.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C28)

questions.q: The drive trades through the first 5-minute high at 9:36. You wait for that 5-minute bar to close up there before you buy.
questions.why: False. You buy at market the moment it trades through. I don't wait for a bar to close. A real drive moves fast. By the time the bar closes, price can be well past the trigger. Your stop is still down under the low of the day, so now it's further away. That means fewer shares for the same risk, on a trade that was already working. The trade through is the signal. The close is just a report on what happened.
questions.lesson_line: The trade through is the trigger. A close is a report, not a signal.
questions.simple: False, you buy at market the moment it trades through. Waiting for the close just costs you size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57)

deeper.example: Lance Breitstein says the same about his own trading: he doesn't wait for bar closes, not for entries and not for exits.

questions.q: A stock sits under its 200-day. It gaps up and the first 5-minute bar is green on huge volume, still under the line. Do you take it?
questions.why: No. Under the 200-day we don't buy stocks. That's a hard line, and a green bar on huge volume doesn't change it. A stock under its 200-day is in a downtrend. Plenty of people bought it higher and are happy to sell into any pop. So a gap there is often just a bounce into sellers. Half size is still a long in a stock we don't buy. The only exception we make is indexes and levered ETFs, never a single stock. I want price over the 200-day, and I like the line rising too.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, there's no drive to buy. Big volume doesn't buy an exception.

wrong.No, the volume's too heavy: Heavy volume is a plus on a drive. The problem is the 200-day.
wrong.Yes, but only half size: Half size is still a buy, in a stock we don't own under the 200-day.
wrong.Yes, if the 200-day is rising: A rising line doesn't help when price is under it. Price has to be over the line.

questions.simple: No. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day, however good the first bar looks.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)

questions.q: A stock with an RS rating of 84 sits in one of the market's strongest groups. It passes as a leader for a drive.
questions.why: True. We buy leaders, and our line is an RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. 84 in a top group clears both. Here's why it matters on a drive. A gap on a leader has buyers already lined up behind it. A gap on a laggard is mostly holders getting out at a better price. Both parts count, though. A high rating in a dead group isn't the same stock. Check the rating the night before, not after the trigger fires.
questions.lesson_line: Drives belong to leaders. RS 80 or more, in a strong group.
questions.simple: True. We want an RS rating of 80 or more in a strong group, and 84 in a top group clears it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C31)

questions.q: At 9:36 price ticks a cent over the first bar's high. The 9:35 bar has not closed. Do you buy?
choices: Yes; the trade through is the trigger
No; wait for the 9:35 bar to close
No; wait for three closed bars
Yes, but only with a limit order
questions.answer: Yes; the trade through is the trigger
questions.why: Yes. The trade through is the trigger, bought at market. We do not wait for a close, and entries are market orders.
questions.lesson_line: A close tells you what already happened. The trade through fires the buy.

wrong.No; wait for the 9:35 bar to close: Waiting for the close is chasing. The card says no waiting for the bar to close.
wrong.No; wait for three closed bars: Three closed bars would leave the drive far behind you. The card buys the trade through.
wrong.Yes, but only with a limit order: Entries are market orders. A limit can miss the break and leave you watching.

questions.q: A good opening drive gets going right at the bell. A stock that sits flat for 5 or 6 minutes first is the unusual case.
questions.why: True. A real drive shows its hand at the bell. The buyers are there right away, and they don't wait around. That's why the low of the day sits at the open or inside the first 5-minute bar. A stock that sits flat for 5 or 6 minutes is thinking, not driving. It might still work later as an opening range breakout. That's a different trade with a different trigger. Don't force a drive onto a slow open.
questions.lesson_line: A good drive starts at the bell. A slow start is a different trade.
questions.simple: True, good drives start at the bell. A stock that stalls for minutes first isn't driving.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)
the 5-minute window is the unit's definition while D-031 is held

deeper.example: SMB, the desk that named the play, puts it the same way: when there's going to be a good opening drive it happens right away, and a delay of 5 to 6 minutes is unusual.

questions.q: The first 5-minute bar closes green, but on less volume than that bar normally trades. How do you treat it?
choices: Still a drive, just a lower grade
Not a drive, skip it completely
Top grade, a calm open's a good sign
questions.answer: Still a drive, just a lower grade
questions.why: Still a drive, just a lower grade. Volume raises the grade. It isn't a must. A first bar on heavy volume tells you real money showed up at the bell, and that's what I want to see. A thin bar says fewer people care today, so it's not one I'd press. The price action still decides whether it's a drive. Green bar, no trade back to the open, buy through the high. Thin volume costs you grade, not the whole trade.
questions.lesson_line: Volume raises the grade. A thin first bar is a lower grade, not a veto.

wrong.Not a drive, skip it completely: Too strict. Volume raises the grade. It doesn't make or break the setup.
wrong.Top grade, a calm open's a good sign: Backwards. Heavy volume at the bell raises the grade. Thin volume lowers it.
wrong.Volume doesn't matter at all: It matters. It's just not a must. It moves the grade up or down.

questions.simple: Still a drive, but a lower grade. Volume raises the grade, it isn't a must.

reasons: the volume floor is a proposed card line tied to held decision D-006

deeper.counter: Zarattini and his co-authors tested opening range breaks on 5-minute bars. Below 100% relative volume the trades averaged -0.02R. That's one study, and it's why thin volume costs grade even though it still counts as a drive.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A drive day that closes in the ___ third of its range has failed.
questions.why: Bottom. A drive day that closes in the bottom third of its range, or below its open, has failed. It is a warning, not a sell signal: the stop is the only exit, and it only moves up. The check grades the day; it does not add a second exit.
questions.lesson_line: Where the day closes grades the drive. The bottom third is a failed one.
questions.simple: Bottom, because a drive day that closes in its bottom third has failed and is a warning sign.

reasons: the day-1 close check was settled by the owner as a warning (D-136)

questions.q: A stock reported last night and gaps up. At 9:35 it drives through the first 5-minute high. Does the earnings rule stop you?
choices: Yes, no buys on report day
questions.why: No, the report's behind it. Our earnings rule looks forward: no new buys in the 3 sessions before a report. The reason is the gamble. You don't want a fresh position with a tight stop sitting through a number nobody knows. A stop can't catch an overnight gap. Here the report's already out and the market has voted. The gap day is fair game for a drive. Holding through the next report is the other half: only if you're up 5R by then.
questions.lesson_line: The earnings rule looks ahead. Once the report's out, the drive is fair game.

wrong.Yes, no buys on report day: The blackout is the 3 sessions before a report. Once it's out, the drive is allowed.
wrong.Yes, wait 3 sessions after: The 3 sessions come before a report, not after. Nothing makes you wait now.
wrong.No, it only covers holding: It covers buying too, in the 3 sessions before. Here the report is already out.

questions.simple: No. The rule only blocks new buys in the 3 days before a report, and this one is already out.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the earnings rule both ways. It only looks forward: no new buys in the 3 sessions before a report. The gap day after the report is open for a drive. Holding through the next report is the other half, and only if the trade is up 5R by then.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: You're in a drive, and by 1:00 it's slipping toward your stop. Moving the stop a bit lower to give it room is fine.
questions.why: False. The stop only moves up. Once you're in, it never goes lower and never gets wider. You set that stop with a clear head before the buy. It's where you decided the drive was wrong. Moving it now is deciding again with your money on the line. That's how a small loss turns into a big one. It's a real stop order with your broker, so it does its job even when you don't want it to. If the dip holds above it, you do nothing.
questions.lesson_line: The stop only moves up. A stop you widen is a stop you stopped believing.
questions.simple: False, the stop only goes up. Widening it turns a small planned loss into a bigger one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, D41)

questions.q: Before the open you check the market reading in our app: Green, Yellow, Orange or Red. Which one lets you take drives at full risk?
questions.why: Green. The market reading is our market filter, and the color tells you how much to trade. Green is full risk for the grade. Yellow is smaller and fewer. Orange is A+ setups only. Red is mostly cash. It's a guide, not a switch. Why it matters: a drive is a bet that buyers keep coming after the bell. In a strong market they do. In a weak one even clean drives get sold, so you size down before the stock ever tells you.
questions.lesson_line: Check the market before the stock. Green is full risk, Red is mostly cash.

wrong.Yellow: Yellow means smaller and fewer. You're trading, just not at full risk.
wrong.Orange: Orange is the A+ setups only. Not a day to press.
wrong.Red: Red is mostly cash. That's not the day to take drives at full risk.

questions.simple: Green. That's the only reading where we trade at full risk.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, a guide)

questions.q: How far is your stop from the fill, in percent?
questions.why: 1.06%. 61.41 minus 60.76 is 0.65 a share. 0.65 over 61.41 is 1.06%. That's a tight stop, right in the 1 to 3% I like. I'll go up to 5% if that's where the chart puts it. A first bar this tight is one of the best things about a drive. The stop is close, so the same dollar risk buys you more shares. RPRX gave you exactly that here. Always work the percent out before you size.
questions.lesson_line: Know your stop in percent before you size. A tight first bar gives you a close stop.
questions.simple: 1.06 percent. Take the fill minus the stop, then divide by the fill.

reasons: computed key
stop width is tied to held decision D-005 and the rulebook's A13

wrong.0.65%: That's the dollar gap, 0.65 a share. You still have to divide by the fill.
wrong.10.58%: Decimal slip. It's about one percent, not ten.
wrong.98.94%: That's how much of the fill is left at the stop, not the gap to it.

questions.story: The first 5-minute bar's high is 61.40. You get filled at 61.41, and the low of the day puts your stop at 60.76.

questions.q: Yesterday closed green. Nothing takes out the first 5-minute high this morning. At 10:05 price breaks the 9:30 to 10:00 high. What is it?
questions.why: The ORB, the opening range breakout. It waits for the whole first half hour, 9:30 to 10:00, and buys the break of that range after 10:00. A drive doesn't wait. It sets the low of the day in the first 5-minute bar and gets bought over that bar's high, by about 9:40. Same kind of morning, different speed. The clock tells you which one you're in. Here nothing broke before 10:00, so there was never a drive to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Check the clock. Over the first bar by 9:40 is a drive. After 10:00, it's the ORB.

wrong.The opening drive: A drive is bought over the first 5-minute high, by about 9:40. This one waited till 10:05.
wrong.A Kicker: A Kicker needs a real red day before the gap. Yesterday closed green.
wrong.The drive's second entry: The second entry comes after a drive fires. No drive fired here.

questions.simple: The ORB. It buys the break of the first half hour after 10:00, while a drive is bought by about 9:40.

reasons: the drive-or-ORB tell is a proposed card line tied to held decision D-031

questions.q: Before it triggers, the stock slips under VWAP, the day's average price, and stays there. Taking the drive at half size is still okay.
questions.why: False. That's not a drive anymore, so the right size is zero. VWAP is the average price everyone has paid today, weighted by volume. A stock holding under it means the average buyer today is losing money. Those people sell into any bounce. A drive is the opposite: buyers in charge from the bell. Half size feels careful, but size is for good setups. It doesn't fix a broken one. After you're in, a lost VWAP is only a warning, and the stop does the selling.
questions.lesson_line: VWAP lost before you buy is a pass. VWAP lost after you buy is a warning.
questions.simple: False, a drive that loses VWAP before you buy has failed. The right size is zero.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating size as the fix. Half size feels careful, but a drive that lost VWAP before the entry isn't a drive. Lance Breitstein's VWAP rule points the same way: never be long a stock steadily holding below VWAP unless it capitulates.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)

questions.q: Your drive is up 2R by noon on the day you bought it. When do you start selling?
questions.why: Day 3 or later, by judgment. I very rarely sell on the day I buy. The money in a drive comes from the days after. I'm after a 3, 5 or 7 day push, often 5 to 10R. Sell at 2R on day one and you cap your best trades at 2R, while your losers still cost a full 1R. That math doesn't work. So you let it run. Think about moving the stop to breakeven somewhere between 2R and 5R, and pick your first sell into the push.
questions.lesson_line: The first sell is a judgment, most often day 3 or later. Rarely day one.

wrong.Right now, take the 2R: That's selling the trade before it can pay. We very rarely sell on day one.
wrong.Into today's close: Still day one. Up 2R by noon isn't a reason to sell.
wrong.On the first red 5-minute candle: One red candle is noise, not a sell signal.

questions.simple: Day 3 or later, by judgment. The big money in a drive comes in the days after, not on day one.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: Your drive is up 1R by 10:15. Time to move the stop up to breakeven.
questions.why: False. Too early. We move the stop to breakeven somewhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell, and even that's a judgment. At 1R your stop is still close to the normal wiggle of the morning. After a strong drive I want to see a pull in on light volume that holds VWAP. A breakeven stop at 1R gets you shaken out on exactly that kind of healthy pullback. Give it room to work first, then protect it.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, not at 1R.
questions.simple: False, breakeven comes somewhere from 2R to 5R, or at the first sell. At 1R it's too early.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19); the card's 'at the first trim by default' is left to the owner

questions.q: It's a $7 stock trading $12 million a day, and the first 5-minute bar is perfect. You can take this drive.
questions.why: False. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that do at least $20 million a day. This one fails both. A perfect bar doesn't fix that. On a thin name the spread is wide, so your market order fills worse than the chart shows. And when you need out, your stop can slip right through. Liquidity is a gate you check before you ever look at the bar.
questions.lesson_line: Liquidity first, chart second. Under $10 or $20 million a day is out.
questions.simple: False, we only trade stocks at $10 or more that do $20 million a day. This one fails both.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: Where's 3R on this trade?

questions.q: Which setup are you trading?
questions.story: A leader sitting in a base gaps up 4.7% after a green day. There's no news you can find, and everybody already watches it. The first 5-minute bar closes green on heavy volume, and price trades through its high.
questions.why: The opening drive. Name the setup before you size it, because each one has its own rules. An EP, an Episodic Pivot, is a big gap on real news in a stock nobody was paying attention to. This has no news, and everyone knows the name. A Kicker needs a real red day before the gap, and yesterday was green. A Parabolic Short needs a burst of straight up days, not a quiet base. None of those fit. So it's a drive, and you trade it like one.
questions.lesson_line: Name the setup before you trade it. No news, no red day, no burst: it's a drive.

wrong.An Episodic Pivot: An EP needs real news on a neglected name. This one has neither.
wrong.A Kicker: A Kicker needs a red day before the gap. Yesterday was green.
wrong.A Parabolic Short: That needs a parabolic burst. This stock gapped out of a quiet base.

questions.simple: The opening drive. No news means no EP, and a green day before means no Kicker.

deeper.trap: The trap is the size of the gap. A big gap on heavy volume can look like an EP. But an EP is real news in a neglected name. Miss either and it's not one. Here no EP, Kicker or burst fits, so the drive's rules read it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)
the gap floor is a held decision (D-134)

questions.q: Whose rules do you trade it by?
questions.story: A Kicker is on your focus list: a real red day yesterday, and this morning it gaps up. It drives straight up from the 9:30 bell.
choices: The drive's, stop at the low of day
questions.why: The Kicker's, stop rule and all. A Kicker that drives from the bell is both setups at once, and when that happens the Kicker's rules win. It's on your list as a Kicker. That's the plan you wrote before the open, and the plan you wrote is the one you trade. Don't shop between the two for the stop you like better. And it's no reason to skip. Two setups lining up on one stock is a good thing.
questions.lesson_line: When a Kicker drives, the Kicker's rules win, stop rule included.

wrong.The drive's, stop at the low of day: When a Kicker drives, the Kicker's rules win, its stop rule included.
wrong.Neither, two setups means skip: Two setups agreeing isn't a reason to skip. Trade it as the Kicker.
wrong.Whichever stop is tighter: Picking the stop you like best is how plans fall apart. The Kicker's rules decide.

questions.simple: The Kicker's rules. When a Kicker drives from the bell, the Kicker's plan is the one you trade.

deeper.trap: The trap is using the drive's stop because the drive came first. When a Kicker drives from the bell, the Kicker's rules win. So the plan carries the Kicker's own stop rule, not just the drive's stop under the low of the day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)
the setup's role is a held decision (D-002)

questions.q: Long or short setup?
questions.story: Three straight up days and two overnight gap-ups, with growing candles. On day 4 it gaps again and drives hard from the bell on a euphoric open.
choices: The U-Turn short setup, not a long
questions.answer: The U-Turn short setup, not a long
questions.why: The U-Turn short setup, not a long. A euphoric drive on day 3 to 5 of a burst, with growing candles, is the climax. It belongs to the Parabolic Short.
questions.lesson_line: Count the up days. A euphoric drive on day 3 to 5 is the short setup.

wrong.A drive; buy the 5-minute high: A euphoric drive on day 3 to 5 of a burst is the short setup, not a long.
wrong.A drive at half size: Half size on a climax is still a long into the top.

questions.q: What do you tell him?
questions.story: A leader above its 200-day gaps up and climbs at a steady slope. The candles get smaller and price hugs its short-term average. A friend wants to short the strength.
choices: Don't fade it, let it run
Short it at the first bar's high
Short it if it loses VWAP
questions.answer: Don't fade it, let it run
questions.why: Don't fade it. Look at what the chart is saying. Steady slope, candles getting smaller, price hugging its short average. That's a calm, strong trend, not a stock running out of gas. Sellers aren't showing up anywhere. Shorting that is stepping in front of it, and those losses are completely avoidable. We don't short a stock above its 200-day unless it's parabolic, and this isn't. If anything, that's the kind of open you want to be long.
questions.lesson_line: A steady drive is a trend to respect. Fading it is the avoidable loss.

wrong.Short the first red candle: One red candle in a steady trend is a breather, not a top.
wrong.Short it at the first bar's high: That's where we'd buy it. Selling there is fighting the trend.
wrong.Short it if it loses VWAP: We don't short above the 200-day unless it's parabolic. This one's a steady leader.

questions.simple: Don't short it. A steady climb with shrinking candles is a strong trend, and fighting that trend costs you for nothing.

deeper.trap: Lance Breitstein's marks of a steady drive: the slope is consistent, about a 1:1 angle upward, and candle size contracts over time. Of one such drive he wrote there was no logical short setup, and losses from fighting this trend were entirely avoidable.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)

questions.q: Do you add to it?
questions.story: It's 9:50 and your drive is up 1R. It looks like it's trending, and you're tempted to add more shares.
choices: Yes, add half on the first dip
No, full size at one price
No, sell a third right now
questions.answer: No, full size at one price
questions.why: No. We buy the full size once, at one price, with one stop. At 9:50, up 1R is a drive doing its job. It isn't a trend yet. In the first 30 minutes a stock pushes, it doesn't trend. Adding to a winner on strength is rare and a feel call, never the plan, and never in the first 30 minutes. Add here and your average price climbs while your stop stays put. Then a normal pullback that was harmless costs you real money. And up 1R on day one isn't a reason to sell either.
questions.lesson_line: A drive isn't a trend yet. Full size at one price, no adding this early.

wrong.Yes, add half on the first dip: Adding in the first 30 minutes mistakes a drive for a trend.
wrong.Yes, add a third at 2R: A planned add at 2R is scaling in. Adding is never the plan.
wrong.No, sell a third right now: Selling on day one is rare. The first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later.

questions.simple: No. You buy the full size once at one price, and a drive this early isn't a trend yet.

deeper.example: SMB, the desk that named the play, warns about this exact mistake: on the open we trade the momentum, and we do not trust trends in the first 30 minutes. Be careful about confusing an opening drive for a stock trending.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)

questions.q: Which grades higher?
questions.story: Two drives on the same daily setup. One's first bar runs 1.6x its normal volume. The other runs 5.3x and trades its average daily volume by 9:45.
questions.why: The 5.3x drive. Average daily volume traded within the first 15 to 30 minutes is an A+ mark. CNC's 5.3x was the heaviest first bar in our set.
questions.lesson_line: Heavier first-bar volume and a full day's average by 9:45 grade the drive up.

wrong.The 1.6x drive: The lighter drive lacks the A+ volume marks.
wrong.They grade the same: Volume grades the drive. The 5.3x one earns the A+ mark.

questions.q: How do you grade that loss?
questions.story: You buy a drive at 216.48 with the stop at 214.23, under the low of the day. It gets to 2.1R by 9:50, then falls through its open and takes your stop.
choices: A reason to widen the next stop
A broken rule, the stop was tight
questions.why: The plan working. You lost 1R, exactly what you signed up for at the buy. The stop under the low of the day took it. It stings because it was up 2.1R at 9:50. But that was day one, when we very rarely sell, so that 2.1R was never yours. Losses like this are part of the deal, and the drives that work pay for them. Don't widen the next stop because of this one. A wider stop doesn't fix anything. It just makes the next loser bigger.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is the plan, not a mistake. The loss was set the moment you bought.

wrong.A reason to widen the next stop: The stop only moves up, and a wider stop just makes the next loser bigger.
wrong.A broken rule, the stop was tight: The stop sat under the low of the day, right where it goes. No rule was broken.
wrong.Proof the setup doesn't work: One stop-out says nothing about a setup. It was the 1R you planned.

questions.simple: The plan working. The stop sat where it belongs, and you lost the 1R you planned.

deeper.trap: The trap is the 2.1R that came first. It feels like a winner thrown away, so traders widen the next stop or give up on the setup. Neither fixes anything. Day one is rarely a sell day, and the stop did its job: the loss was the 1R set at the buy.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)

questions.q: Do you sell it here?
questions.story: EAT, 2026-09-22. You bought at 9:40. The high prints at 9:45, a lower high follows, and at 9:55 it closes under VWAP for the first time.
choices: No, hold, the stop's the exit
Add more shares on this dip
Widen the stop to give it room
questions.answer: No, hold, the stop's the exit
questions.why: Hold. The stop is the exit. Losing VWAP after you're in is a warning, and I'll be watching it closely, but I don't sell on it. The stop is already sitting with the broker, under the low of the day. If the drive is really done, it'll get hit and you lose what you planned. EAT took its stop at 14:20 and closed at 24% of its range. The loss was the one sized at the buy, no worse. What you don't do is add into it or widen the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Lose VWAP after you buy and it's a warning. The stop does the selling.

wrong.Add more shares on this dip: Never into a failing drive. That's the worst add there is.
wrong.Widen the stop to give it room: The stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Yes, sell now at market: After the entry a lost VWAP is a warning only. The stop does the selling.

questions.simple: Hold and let the stop do the selling. A lost VWAP after you buy is a warning, not an exit.

deeper.trap: On EAT the warning came at 9:55 and the stop at 14:20. Read in hindsight, selling at the warning looks clever. Our rule keeps the stop as the one exit, so the loss is the one sized at the buy. The plan never depends on reading each warning right in the moment.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)
follows a held decision (D-136)

questions.q: Can you get back in?
questions.story: You bought a drive at 9:35, and the fill turned out to be the high of the day. It slid for an hour and took your stop at 10:35. You still like the daily chart.
choices: Only on a new trigger and stop
Only after a full day passes
Yes, with a wider stop this time
questions.answer: Only on a new trigger and stop
questions.why: Only on a new trigger. A stop-out ends the trade, and liking the chart isn't a trigger. Say the setup triggers again, a fresh pullback that holds VWAP and breaks back up. That's a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Not before. Jumping straight back in is how one loss turns into three in a morning. And every try counts. On one stock we take at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out ends the trade. A new trigger is a new trade with its own stop.

wrong.Yes, with a wider stop this time: The stop never gets wider, and you still need a new trigger first.
wrong.Only after a full day passes: Time isn't a trigger. Only the setup triggering again lets you back in.
wrong.No, not this month: You can go again on a new trigger. It just counts toward 3 tries a week and 6 a month.

questions.simple: Only on a new trigger. A stop-out ends the trade, and any new buy is a new trade with its own stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is the urge to get straight back in. PAYC filled at the high of the day at 9:35, slid for an hour and took the stop at 10:35. Without a new trigger and a new stop, buying it back is a guess, not a trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21, E56)
fixed before

questions.q: What's your play this morning?
questions.story: Our market filter reads Red, the weakest of its four colors. At 9:35 four drives fire at once, all clean first bars on heavy volume.
choices: Mostly longs, the bars are clean
The best one at full risk
questions.why: Mostly cash. Red means the market is in bad shape, and in Red we're mostly cash, plus shorts in stocks under their 200-day. It's a guide, not a switch, but clean bars don't change it. A drive needs buyers to keep showing up after the bell. In a weak market they don't stick around, and good-looking setups fail together. It happens: on 2026-10-06 four strict drives fired the same morning and all four got stopped. Shorting these isn't the answer either. They're long setups.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market first. In Red, clean drives don't change the answer.

wrong.Mostly longs, the bars are clean: Clean bars don't change the reading. Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Short all four drives: Red's shorts are stocks under their 200-day. These are long setups.
wrong.The best one at full risk: Full risk is for Green. In Red you're mostly cash.

questions.simple: Mostly cash. In a Red market even clean drives fail together, so you sit most of it out.

deeper.example: RVTY, 2026-10-06: bought 165.00 at 9:35 with the stop at 161.45, stopped at 9:50. NVT, ARKG and CIBR fired the same morning, and all four were stopped. The drives were real for five minutes and the market was not. This example doesn't say the day read Red. It shows how much the market weighs on a clean bar.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)

questions.q: Last autumn our scan found 41 strict drives in 59 sessions. How many do you think got stopped out the same day?
questions.why: About four in ten. 41.5% were stopped on the drive day itself, and 87.8% were stopped within 20 sessions. Only 17.1% got to 3R and 9.8% to 5R before the stop. Those are fixed-stop numbers, with no sells and no breakeven move. The point still stands: you will lose on drives a lot. That's fine when the losses are small and the winners run. Plan for it before the bell, so a stop-out doesn't rattle you. It's one autumn, 41 trades on 21 days, so read it as a feel, not a forecast.
questions.lesson_line: Plan on losing often. Keep the losses small and let the few winners pay.

wrong.About one in ten: Far more than that. 41.5% were stopped the same day.
wrong.About nine in ten: That's the 20-session number, 87.8%. On the drive day it was 41.5%.
wrong.About six in ten: Fewer. 41.5% went on the drive day, under half.

questions.simple: About four in ten. Plenty of drives fail the same day, so plan for small losses.

deeper.counter: The 41 came on only 21 different days, so many fired on the same mornings. It's one window and one market. The scan's strict test also used numbers that aren't our rules, so read it as a sample, not a law.

reasons: scan statistics from one 59-session window can change
the strict rule includes pending decisions D-134 and D-006
fixed before

questions.q: What is the entry?
questions.story: You missed the 9:35 break. At 10:45 the stock pulls back on lighter volume, holds VWAP and stays above the first bar's high.
choices: Skip; a missed 9:35 break is gone
A break over the pullback's high
Market now, stop under the low
questions.answer: A break over the pullback's high
questions.why: A break back over the pullback's high. That is the card's second entry. After the drive, it is the first pullback on lighter volume that holds above VWAP and the opening-range high or the open. Buy the break back over its high. The card puts the stop a few cents under the pullback's low. Missing 9:35 does not end the setup. Our own trading notes say to look for a retest or an undercut and hold of VWAP mid morning.
questions.lesson_line: Wait for the pullback to prove itself, then buy its break. Our card puts the stop under the pullback low.

wrong.Skip; a missed 9:35 break is gone: A first pullback that holds VWAP is the second entry. The setup is still on.
wrong.Market now, stop under the low: The second entry buys the break back over the pullback's high, not a market order mid-pullback.
wrong.Buy at tomorrow's open instead: The second entry is today's first light pullback that holds VWAP, bought on the break of its high.

questions.simple: Buy when it breaks back over the pullback's high, because a light pullback that holds VWAP is the second way in.

deeper.trap: The trap is the clock. Missing 9:35 feels like missing the trade, so traders either chase or quit. The card's second entry needs no clock. It is the first pullback on lighter volume that holds VWAP and the opening-range high or the open. Buy the break back over the pullback's high.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)

questions.q: A stock under its 200-day drives on a gap up the day after a hard burst down. Even as a parabolic long, it's a pass.
questions.why: True. Under the 200-day is a hard no for stocks. The one exception is indexes and levered ETFs. We can buy those under the line on a reversal or a parabolic long, a gap that drives after a burst down. A single stock doesn't get that pass, however good the drive looks. An index comes back when the market comes back. A broken stock can stay broken for reasons that have nothing to do with the market.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day is a hard no for stocks. Only indexes and levered ETFs get a pass.
questions.simple: True, only indexes and levered ETFs can be bought under the 200-day. A stock never gets that pass.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the parabolic long as a door for any stock. Below the 200-day a stock is no trade, however clean the drive. The gap-and-drive after a burst down is a long we take only in an index or a levered ETF.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)

questions.q: Which plan do you write down before it triggers?
questions.story: LRCX, 2026-09-18. A leader, RS 82, over its 200-day. The first 5-minute bar runs 272.80 to 277.23 on 5.7x volume. It dips first, then closes green.
questions.why: Market 277.24, stop 272.75, first sell day 3 or later. The trigger is the first trade through 277.23, so your market order fills around 277.24. The low of the day is the first bar's low, 272.80, and the stop goes a few cents under it at 272.75. That's 1.6% away, nice and tight. Then the first sell is a judgment, and I very rarely make it on day one. LRCX hit 3R at the next morning's open and ran to 16.8R at its best. Sell on day one and you've thrown away the part that pays.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, first sell. Write it before the bell, then just execute.

wrong.Limit 275.00, stop 268.00, sell at 2R: A limit under the trigger won't fill on the break, and 268.00 is nowhere near the low of the day.
wrong.Buy the 9:40 close, stop 272.80, hold: The trigger is the trade through, not a bar close. And the stop goes under the low, not on it.
wrong.Market 277.24, stop 272.75, sell day one: Right entry, right stop. But we very rarely sell on day one, and this one ran to 16.8R.

questions.simple: Buy at market through 277.23, stop just under 272.80, and make the first sell on day 3 or later.

deeper.trap: Two plans here share the entry and the stop. The difference is the first sell. Selling on day one throws away the part that pays: LRCX went on to 16.8R at its best. The first sell waits for the push, and the rest trails.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, F62, B19, E51)
computed key (entry and stop derived from the bar)

questions.q: What does the gap rule say?
questions.story: SANM, 2026-09-11: you bought at 208.00 with the stop at 205.66 and sold a third at 3R. On 09-14 the stock gaps down through the stop.
choices: Buy more at the lower price
30-minute low is the stop; cap at 2R
Sell at the open, no questions
Hold; the third banked covers it
questions.answer: 30-minute low is the stop; cap at 2R
questions.why: The first 30-minute low is the new stop, and if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out. The third sold at 3R was already banked.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide, under a 2R cap.

wrong.Sell at the open, no questions: The gap rule gives the first 30 minutes the decision, under the 2R cap.
wrong.Hold; the third banked covers it: The banked third does not move the stop. The 30-minute low does.
wrong.Buy more at the lower price: Full size at one price with one stop, no adding.

questions.q: You're long from 208.00 with the stop at 205.66. The next morning it gaps open under your stop. At what price is your loss 2R?
questions.why: 203.32. 208.00 minus 205.66 is 2.34, and that's 1R. Two of them is 4.68. Take that off your fill and you're at 203.32. Here's why you want that number before the open. On a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar becomes your new stop. If those first 30 minutes take you past 2R, under 203.32, you're out. Know the line ahead of time and there's nothing to decide in the panic.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 2R price before the gap. The first 30 minutes decide.
questions.simple: 203.32. One R is the fill minus the stop, and the 2R line sits two of those under the fill.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating the gap rule as a free pass. A gap below 205.66 doesn't mean you sell at the open, and it doesn't mean you wait all day. The low of the first 30-minute bar becomes the stop, with a ceiling: if those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, below 203.32, you're out.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B20)

wrong.$200.98: You counted 2R down from the stop. Count it from your fill.
wrong.$212.68: That's 2R up. A loss goes down from the fill.
wrong.$205.66: That's your old stop, a 1R loss.

questions.q: SMB runs the drive as a scalp with its own quick exits. We swing trade our drives, so those scalp exits aren't ours.
questions.why: True. SMB is a day-trading desk. They say you're either in a scalp, with all its specific exits, or a hold plan. Their scalp exits fit their game. Ours is swing trading, holding for days to a few weeks. So our first sell is a judgment. Very rarely day one, more often day 3 or later, into a 3, 5 or 7 day push. Then the rest trails. Borrow their entry if you like. Take their exits and you'll scalp your best swing trades away.
questions.lesson_line: SMB's scalp exits aren't ours. We sell into the push and trail the rest.
questions.simple: True. We swing trade, so we sell into a push over several days and trail the rest.

deeper.trap: The trap is taking a scalp's exits on a swing drive. SMB's scalp exits belong to its scalp plan, not ours. Ours are swing exits: a first sell by judgment, into a 3 to 7 day push, then a trail on the rest.

reasons: day trade or swing is held decision D-002
fixed before

questions.q: SMB says on a drive you're either in a scalp or a hold plan, picked up front. Which of these is the mistake?
choices: A hard stop on a scalp
Picking a scalp on the open
questions.why: Switching plans mid-trade. You pick the plan before you buy, and you keep it. The switch is where it goes wrong. You planned a hold, it dips, and you scalp it for a small loss. Or you planned a scalp, it runs, and you hold it all the way back down. Either way you're deciding with money on the line instead of with a clear head. We work the same way: entry, stop and size get written down before the market opens.
questions.lesson_line: Pick the plan before you buy. Changing it mid-trade is the mistake.

wrong.Picking a scalp on the open: SMB's warning runs the other way. A hold almost never starts on the open, because stocks don't trend there.
wrong.Picking the plan before entry: That's exactly right. Entry, stop and size are written down before the open.
wrong.A hard stop on a scalp: Every plan has a stop, a real order with the broker.

questions.simple: Switching plans mid-trade. You set the plan before you buy, then you stick with it.

deeper.trap: Borrowing SMB's play brings a quiet risk: taking their scalp exit on a trade you planned as a swing. That's the switch to watch for. We swing trade, so the plan is set before the buy, and the exits are our sells and the trail.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)

questions.q: Where is the first trim taken?
questions.story: You hold a drive with the first trim at 3R. The next morning the stock opens above 3R.
choices: At the open; the level is passed
At the old 3R price, with a limit
Wait for it to come back to 3R
questions.answer: At the open; the level is passed
questions.why: At the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, 3R or 5R, take that trim at the open. The level is behind you, so waiting for it or parking a limit there is hope, not the plan. LRCX and STX reached 3R at the next session's open. The first 30-minute low belongs to the gap-down stop rule, not a gap up.
questions.lesson_line: A level the day opens past is taken at the open. Do not wait for a price that is gone.

wrong.At the old 3R price, with a limit: That price is behind you. The trim is taken at the open.
wrong.At the first 30-minute low: That is the gap-down stop rule. This is a gap up through a trim.
wrong.Wait for it to come back to 3R: Waiting for a level that has passed is hope, not a rule. Take the trim at the open.

questions.simple: Take the trim at the open, because the stock already opened past 3R and that price may not come back.

deeper.example: LRCX: bought 277.24 on 2026-09-18 with the stop at 272.75. It reached 3R at the next session's open, 09-21 at 9:30. Under our rule, the first third comes off at that open. 5R came at 11:40 that day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook or a card proposal under owner review (house)

questions.q: A drive fills at 96.97. Its 10-day average is 88.31. How far is the fill above the 10-day, in percent?
questions.why: 9.81%, just inside the 10% line. That is MXL's case: 9.8% over its 10-day, the edge of the stretch rule, and it ran 5.2R at its best.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stretch against the 10-day. Past 10% over, the long is skipped.

questions.q: Your drive is in a stock that trades 850,000 shares a day on average. What's the most shares we'd own in it?
questions.why: 8,500 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. 850,000 times 0.01 is 8,500. That's a ceiling, not a target, and your risk math will most often land under it. Here's why it exists. If you own a big chunk of what trades in a day, you can't get out fast when you need to. Your own selling pushes the price against you. It's the same reason we don't even watch illiquid names.
questions.lesson_line: Size to the volume. One percent of an average day is the ceiling.
questions.simple: 8,500 shares. We never own more than 1 percent of a stock's average daily volume.

reasons: computed key
rests on the owner's rulebook (D42)

wrong.85,000 shares: The decimal moved one place too far. That's ten times the ceiling.
wrong.841,500 shares: You took 1% off the volume instead of 1% of it.
wrong.17,000 shares: You doubled it. The ceiling is 1%.

questions.q: Which ones do you take?
questions.story: Six drives on your list this morning. Our market filter reads Orange, one step above Red: the market's under pressure.
questions.why: Only the A+ ones. In an Orange market breakouts fail more often, because the market isn't backing them. So I only want my very best ideas, the cleanest setups with the tightest risk, the kind we size up on. A clean first bar isn't the same as A+. Grading is a judgment call, and if none of the six is A+, nothing on the list gets bought today. Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Mostly cash is Red.
questions.lesson_line: Orange means A+ only. Cut the list to the best before the open.

wrong.Fewer of them, smaller size: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Orange is stricter, A+ only.
wrong.All six, each looks clean: Orange is A+ only. Clean isn't the same as A+.
wrong.None, Orange means no buying: Mostly cash is Red. Orange still lets you take the A+ setups.

questions.simple: Only the A+ ones. In Orange the market isn't backing breakouts, so you take only your best.

questions.q: Which setup does this failed drive belong to?
choices: An Episodic Pivot, a news gap
A Kicker, it gapped up again
questions.why: The Parabolic Short. Day 4 of a run with stacked gap ups is a parabolic burst. A euphoric gap that drives and then fails is the climax. Bracco calls that failed drive the U-Turn. It belongs to the Parabolic Short, the one short we allow above the 200-day, and only because it's parabolic. It's not a drive to hold, and it's not a Kicker, since there's no red day before the gap. Shorting is only for traders who've already made $1 million trading.
questions.lesson_line: On day 3 to 5 of a burst, a failed up-drive is the U-Turn, a climax short.

wrong.The Opening Drive, stay long: On day 3 to 5 of a burst we don't buy the drive. Its failure is the U-Turn short.
wrong.An Episodic Pivot, a news gap: An EP is news on a neglected name. This one's a gap on top of a run.
wrong.A Kicker, it gapped up again: A Kicker needs a red day before the gap. Day 4 of a run of gap ups has none.

questions.story: Day 4 of a run with two overnight gap ups. The stock gaps up again on a euphoric open and drives over its first 5-minute high. By 10:30 it has lost VWAP and broken the low of the day.
questions.simple: The Parabolic Short. A drive that fails on day 4 of a burst is the U-Turn, a climax short.

deeper.trap: The trap is holding the long because it started as a drive. On day 3 to 5 of a burst, a euphoric open is the climax, and we don't buy it at all. Naming the failure as the Parabolic Short's setup turns a trap into a read, under that setup's own rules.

questions.q: A drive day closes in the bottom third of its day's range. What does that tell us?
choices: The drive failed; it is a warning
The drive is strong; add to it
A sell signal; exit at the close
Nothing; only the open grades a drive
questions.answer: The drive failed; it is a warning
questions.why: The drive failed, and that is a warning. A drive day that closes below its open or in the bottom third of its range has failed. It is not a sell signal: the stop is the only exit, and it only moves up. The check grades the day. It adds no second exit.
questions.lesson_line: A bottom-third close grades the drive as failed.

wrong.The drive is strong; add to it: A close in the bottom third is the opposite of strength. Adding to it adds risk to a drive that just failed.
wrong.A sell signal; exit at the close: The stop is the only exit. The close check grades the day. It does not add a second exit.
wrong.Nothing; only the open grades a drive: The close grades the drive too. A drive day that closes in the bottom third of its range has failed.

questions.simple: The drive failed, so treat it as a warning, but the stop stays your only exit.
